## What's new in 0.34.0 (since 0.33.0)

- **Secure by default.** A node that listens beyond its own machine is never open now. With no token, its leader makes the lake's first user, `pondra`, and prints its token once, and `pondra token --dir LAKE` makes another one with the node up or down. A node started by the shell, `local()` or a project command answers only that program, and a lake once served with tokens never opens up again when a node is started on it without them. From another machine a password crosses only TLS, and ten wrong passwords in a minute lock out that address for that user, not everyone. An open node refuses web pages from other sites, so a page you visit can't send it SQL. With an admin token and no `PONDRA_SECRET_KEY`, the token seals the lake's own keys and secrets. The row doors check the INSERT grant (Flight's DoPut and Kafka's produce too, where a user granted one table could write another through Flight), the audit log, the statement history and the run log take no statement's rows and stream to superusers only, a change forwarded to the leader runs as its user, and a user is shown only the tables it may read and routines without their code, in Postgres's catalog too. Wrong passwords are counted on the Postgres port and Flight as on HTTP, and Flight signs a call in before it reads the call's body. A temporary secret made by anyone but an admin reads with its own keys on the public internet only, never the node's credentials, its machine or its network. A secret's `SCOPE` covers a URL only whole or followed by `/`, `?` or `#`, so `s3://data` no longer covers `s3://data-other/`. Loading a table with a primary key through `/append`, Flight, Kafka or `COPY` asks UPDATE as well as INSERT, and rows marked deleted ask DELETE. The installers check the release's SHA-256.
- **Pondra in your process.** `pondra.connect()` is the one way in, in Python and JavaScript. With no argument, or `":memory:"` as DuckDB spells it, it opens a lake held in memory with nothing on disk. A folder or a bucket URL opens that lake with its node in this process, and an `http(s)://` URL reaches a node somewhere. `pondra :memory:` and `pondra serve :memory:` do the same from the command line. A lake in this process answers live queries, watches and big answers through the library, Ctrl-C stops a long query, and closing it takes 0.02 s instead of 0.9 s. The packages carry one library, on jemalloc on Linux as the program is, so `pip install pondra` gives memory back and runs TPC-H as fast as the release archive. Ten million rows reach pandas in 0.92 s, against 1.25 s for DuckDB 1.5.5.
- **The tools you already use.** `pip install pondra sqlalchemy` is the whole install for SQLAlchemy: `create_engine("pondra:///folder")`, `"pondra+http://host:port"` or `"pondra+psycopg://…"`, with the ORM, the inspector, pandas' `to_sql` and `read_sql`, and Alembic. `pondra.dbapi` is the standard Python database API, and `dbt-pondra` is a dbt adapter that keeps keys and layouts in model configs, merges incremental models and leaves materialized views for Pondra to keep current. Every statement Grafana, Metabase, Superset and DBeaver send (211 of them) answers as Postgres 16 answers it, and so do Tableau's and Power BI's. The Postgres port names an answer's columns as Postgres does (`count`, `?column?`) and remembers answers as HTTP does, so a dashboard's repeated TPC-H Q6 runs about 6,000 to 8,000 times a second over the port. `INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE … RETURNING` work at every door, which is how Django, Rails, Prisma and SQLAlchemy learn a new row's key. A `UUID` type checks its values at every door and reaches Postgres clients as `uuid`, with `gen_random_uuid()` and `uuidv7()`.
- **Transactions as Postgres runs them.** READ COMMITTED is now the default: a write locks its rows until its transaction ends, and a second writer waits its turn instead of failing at COMMIT with 40001. `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` locks, `SAVEPOINT` and `ROLLBACK TO` work, and DDL runs inside a transaction, so dbt seeds, pandas `to_sql` and SQLAlchemy's `create_all` work. pgbench with four clients ran 197 transactions a second with none retried, against 141 with 844 retried. MCP and Flight SQL hold transactions across calls. The Postgres port cancels a running statement, keeps cursors (`DECLARE`, `FETCH`, psycopg's named cursors, pgjdbc's fetch size), binds typed parameters and lists enums, sequences and CHECKs in its catalog.
- **Backups.** `BACKUP DATABASE TO 's3://other-bucket/shop'` copies a database as of one moment, and run again it copies only what changed, keeping each run for `retention_days`. A backup reads like any database and refuses every write. `RESTORE DATABASE shop2 FROM '…' AT (TIMESTAMP => '…')` brings a run back with its tasks suspended. `pondra backup` and `pondra restore` do the same with no node running, and a task keeps one nightly.
- **The team's workflow.** `pondra branch add-discounts` makes a Git branch and a database cloned from prod with no file copied. `pondra apply` makes your database match the project's files and runs the tests, and `pondra status` and `pondra capture` show and write back what changed by hand, telling a rename from a drop. Prod can be protected so that only an apply by a holder of `APPLY` changes what a project declared. Dev can branch a prod on another server and another bucket, through a read-only key. `pondra ci init` writes the GitHub workflow that gives each pull request its own database. A workspace folder can be a Git folder (`CALL git_commit('sales', '…')`, `git_pull`, `git_pull_request`), and `ALTER TABLE orders SWAP WITH orders_wap` publishes a table written beside another in one commit.
- **Loading and other catalogs.** `COPY INTO orders FROM 's3://landing/orders/'` loads each file once per version, through retries, two nodes and a kill, and `pondra.loads` lists what it loaded. AWS Glue and S3 Tables attach and are read and written with the secret's keys. REST catalogs such as Polaris, Unity and Lakekeeper hand out credentials that reach only their table's files. A table with a `UNIQUE` now takes rows through HTTP appends, Flight, `COPY FROM STDIN` and Kafka, each batch checked on the leader. A bulk `INSERT … SELECT` or `CREATE TABLE … AS` writes its files a batch at a time on every core: TPC-H's eight tables load from Parquet in 5.2–5.5 s instead of 21–22 s, at half the memory.
- **SQL as newcomers type it.** 281 statements typed as Postgres, DuckDB, Snowflake, Spark, MySQL, BigQuery and SQL Server users type them were tried, and each one either runs or is refused with the statement to write. `USE crm` and `SET search_path` work at every door with a session. `ALTER COLUMN … SET DEFAULT | SET NOT NULL`, `DROP … CASCADE`, several actions in one `ALTER TABLE` and a temporary table's primary key all work. `pondra.parts` lists every part of every object, and `pondra.find('revenue')` searches objects, parts and concepts at once. A DOUBLE that meets a DECIMAL is a DOUBLE, as in Postgres and DuckDB, so `x > 0.5` no longer casts every row and big values no longer fail. `x IN (SELECT …)` and `EXISTS` work outside a WHERE, `avg` over a DECIMAL rounds its last place, two subqueries, a repeated expression or `sum(c)` beside `sum(c::DOUBLE)` in one SELECT are named apart, a JSON or struct field read from a keyed table answers, and `SHOW CREATE` shows a session's temporary tables and views.
- **Faster.** TPC-H SF1 from memory takes 1.08 s, ahead of DuckDB 1.5.5's own tables at 1.15 s, and 2.06 s from Parquet files (DuckDB 2.19 s), each the median of three runs on one 4-core machine. A join's small build side on one integer key is looked up in an array (TPC-H q17 58 ms to 24 ms), and keys a query implies join first (q5 0.74×). Joins are sized from what the tables know, so a filter the planner couldn't size no longer builds a hash table on the bigger side: TPC-DS's 99 queries from memory take 0.85 of the time and TPC-H's 22 0.89. Twenty Nexmark queries as materialized views answer 6 to 14 s after a 2M-event stream ends, where they took 48.8 s. At 10M events Pondra's last answer comes 80 s after the first event, against 685 s for Flink 2.3. A wide top-N (`SELECT * … ORDER BY t LIMIT 10`) skips files by its moving bound and fits a 1.6 GB container. A statement over the Postgres port costs a third less (`SELECT 1` 0.92 ms, 1.36 before) and one-row INSERTs from four clients land 1,558 a second (977). A node's first query costs a third of the instructions it did, planning from memory is up to half as costly, and a lake's only node, once killed, is writable again in 0.1 s instead of 30 s. Under steady small writes a node's memory now levels off instead of growing for as long as it ran.
- **Big answers and busy nodes.** An answer counts in the node's query memory until it is sent, and one too big for it is refused with 53200 instead of taking the node down. Over HTTP an answer of 8 MB or more goes in 1 MB pieces as it is written. A node runs at most `PONDRA_QUERIES` queries at once (four a core) and the rest wait their turn, and one that waits a minute is refused with 53300, which the clients retry. A node counts every request it makes of its bucket in the classes S3 and R2 bill, reads included, and `pondra_cache_bytes` reports every cache it keeps, so its memory can be told from what its bounded caches hold. One node taking 13 MiB/s at R2's latency costs about $121 a month in requests at S3's list prices.
- **Clients.** JavaScript has frames with nodejs-polars' names, which send the same SQL as Python's, and its calls now follow Python's. `pondra.spark` gives PySpark 4.0.1's answer on all 80 checked pipelines, after 16 wrong answers were fixed. The Python client keeps its connections: it appends 4.6 M rows a second (Fluss 1.0: 4.7 M) and looks a key up in 0.28 ms (Fluss: 102 ms). `local()` refuses a port another node holds.
- **Wrong answers and failures fixed.** An attached lake's table could lose or repeat a changed row for a moment after each commit there. A table with a column named `created_at`, `version` or `row_id` couldn't be changed at all. A rename or drop under steady writers could lose an acknowledged row, an `UPDATE` under backpressure could hang the leader, and with views running one run in four stopped every write for good. A follower that started too early answered anyone as an admin. A transaction over 12,000 keys of a keyed table took its node down. dbt's snapshots failed, a new materialized view read empty for a moment, and Delta readers saw writes after 990 ms instead of 57 ms. One table's failed publish stopped the whole tiering round. A leader killed and started again by its service or container opened the lake as leader twice, and writes now wait 7–10 s through it on a bucket as slow as R2, where they waited 12–15 s. `AT (OFFSET => -1)` and `today()` could be answered from memory after the moment moved. Each is fixed, and each has a check.

### Upgrading from 0.33.0

- **A node on the network asks everyone to sign in.** Use the token it prints once, make one with `pondra token --dir LAKE`, or give every node `--admin-token`. A cluster with an admin token and no `PONDRA_SECRET_KEY` needs the same admin token on every node, since that token seals the lake's keys.
- **The lake's format moves** once every node runs 0.34.0, and only when a write needs it: to 3 when the lake's own keys are sealed (by `PONDRA_SECRET_KEY` or a shared admin token, which happens at the leader's first start with one), to 4 with a grant on another database. 0.33.0 then refuses the lake by name: take a backup before upgrading if you may need to go back.
- **Transactions are READ COMMITTED by default,** with writers that wait. `SERIALIZABLE` is refused by name, and `FOR UPDATE` really locks.
- **Errors carry their HTTP status by SQLSTATE:** a bad statement, a table definition refused or a body that can't be read is 400, a missing name 404, a conflict 409, a feature not taken yet 501, a busy or catching-up node 503. Before, almost every error was 500.
- **Refused now, where they were taken quietly:** `--pg`, `--kafka` or `--flight` on a port another program holds (the node no longer starts without that door), an `INSERT INTO` a name no table has (42P01; `CREATE TABLE … AS SELECT` makes one), rows for a table dropped or renamed away (42P01), a `read_*` option given twice, a positional argument after a named one, a value longer than its `VARCHAR(n)` (22001, as Postgres refuses it) and a table with two primary keys (42P16).
- **`connect()` replaces `local()` and `open()`,** which still work, with a warning, until 1.0.
- **Answers over the Postgres port carry Postgres's column names:** `count(*)` is `count`, `1` is `?column?`, a cast takes its type's name. HTTP, Flight and MCP keep the names they had. `avg` over a DECIMAL may differ from 0.33.0 in its last place, now rounded rather than cut off.
- **Secrets:** a temporary secret made by a user who isn't an admin reaches only the public internet. An admin's `CREATE SECRET … SCOPE '…'` with `GRANT USAGE` is the way to private buckets and services. Loads into a table with a primary key need UPDATE as well as INSERT, and deletes through a load need DELETE.
- **Metrics:** `pondra_object_requests_total{op="write"}` now counts each part of a multipart upload, and a scan's reads are counted too (`op="read"`).
- **Renamed:** `deploy` is `apply` (`pondra apply`, `GRANT APPLY`, `pondra.applies`). `pondra dev`, `pondra branch --hook` and `--if-missing` are gone.
- **The planner's learned facts are off by default** (`PONDRA_LEARN=on` turns them on). Runs still learn them, and `pondra.learned` lists them.
- **Clients:** `from pondra import *` no longer replaces Python's `sum`, `len`, `max`, `min` and `all`. JavaScript's `local()` takes `timeout` in seconds. ADBC's Flight SQL connections open a transaction unless `autocommit=True`. A string column is `text` in the Postgres catalog.
- **New settings:** `PONDRA_QUERIES`, `PONDRA_QUEUE_SECS`, `PONDRA_STREAM_MB`, `PONDRA_STATEMENT_TIMEOUT`, `PONDRA_TRUSTED_PROXIES` (set it when your own load balancer fronts the nodes), `PONDRA_TXN_IDLE_SECS`, `PONDRA_BLOCKING_THREADS`.

### Known in 0.34.0

- A `MERGE` whose `ON` doesn't name the table's primary key, run outside a transaction, can replace a row whose key its `WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT` inserts, where Postgres refuses it with 23505. It has been so since `MERGE` came, and the next release refuses it. Until then, put the key in the `ON`.

The details are in each pull request, and the measures in [`logs/gates/`](https://github.com/alimardon123/pondra/tree/main/logs/gates).

## What was new in 0.33.0 (since 0.32.0)

- **Wrong answers fixed.** Two `IN` lists on one column were intersected as if they were sets of values, a `NOT IN (NULL)` beside another list was dropped, a projection pushed through a filter could swap two columns of one name and type, and `- -3` written back as text became a comment. Checked against DuckDB on 100,000 random queries, 99,974 now agree. The other 26 are queries DataFusion refuses and DuckDB doesn't, not wrong answers. A table with an `INTERVAL` column never left the log, and held every other table of its lake there too. It now goes to files like any other, and its intervals read back exactly. A spread read of a history view counted the versions it had deleted, a session window could miss a new key's late row (seen on simulated R2), and a write to an attached lake could be missed by the next statement. All are fixed.
- **Statements that did the wrong thing.** `CREATE TABLE … PARTITION BY` and `CLUSTER BY` used to make a table with neither. They now set the partitions and clustering, and `day(ts)` and `date_trunc('day', ts)` give the same partitions. `INSERT OR IGNORE` and MySQL's `INSERT IGNORE` used to replace the row that was there and now leave it alone. `CREATE TABLE … LIKE` used to make a table with no columns and now copies the columns and types of the table it names.
- **Functions and procedures that answered wrongly.** A SQL function that reads a table took the caller's column of the same name. Now the call is refused when both read a table of one name, and an alias is the way out. Answers kept for `f(1)` and `f(1.0)` were one, and now are kept apart. A view that calls `now()`, reads files or calls a volatile Python function is no longer answered from the result cache. A `FOR` loop retried with its job could write one row twice and skip another when its rows came back in a different order. A function built from other functions now uses their current definitions, not the ones they had when it was made. Calls that would copy too much or write out too many expressions are refused by name, and the node stays up.
- **Each database locked on its own.** A database that has users who sign in is used only through itself or with the nodes' own tokens, so a user signed in next door is nobody there, not even a superuser. Before, `GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES` in one database read another database's tables, and a database with no users let anyone read a locked one beside it. A user granted another database's tables needs a grant that names them, such as `GRANT SELECT ON crm.customers TO ann`. A database with no sign-in at all stays open to anyone. A procedure started with `pondra.start` now runs with its caller's grants. Before, it ran with none, so a user granted nothing on a secret could copy it into a table it could write.
- **Writes survive failures.** In a 4.8-hour run on R2 with three nodes, eight nodes were stopped or killed in turn. Each of 43,138 acknowledged batches was there once, none lost or stored twice, and none of 423,085 reads was torn. A leader cut off from its bucket, while another node is there, now turns writes away at once instead of holding each one until its client gives up. A lake on a small local disk keeps a quarter of the disk free, up to 256 MB. Writes wait with no error when the free room drops below that, and the log drains again once room returns. A lake's format now moves on only when a write needs the new one, so the release before can still open a lake a newer release has only read.
- **Every statement remembered, with its plan.** `SELECT * FROM pondra.history` lists every statement from every door: who ran it, how long it took or how it ended, its rows and how many nodes it ran on. A statement whose client stopped waiting is a row too, with the outcome `stopped`. A slow one (over a second, `PONDRA_SLOW_MS`) keeps the plan that ran, with each step's rows and time and each node's share, and is written to the node's log too. An admin sees everyone's rows, and anyone else sees their own. `EXPLAIN` now gives each step's expected rows, and `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` puts them beside the actual ones. Queries of 100 ms or more note each filter the planner judged off by two times or more, and `pondra.learned` lists those notes. The planner does not use them yet. The console's History tab shows the same rows.
- **Every materialized view stays current.** Any `SELECT` over a lake's tables can now be a materialized view, and it stays current. Pondra picks the cheapest way that is right, and `pondra.flows` shows which. A `GROUP BY` with averages, standard deviations, `HAVING` or `ORDER BY … LIMIT` is kept as partial rows and finished as it is read. `median`, `count(DISTINCT …)` and `string_agg` recompute only the groups whose rows changed, and write those. Anything else runs whole after each commit to a table it reads, and only the rows that differ are written. A view without a `GROUP BY` that used `ORDER BY … LIMIT`, `DISTINCT`, a window or a subquery over its own table answered wrongly before. `WITH (refresh = 'by key')` (or `'incremental'` or `'full'`) asks for one way, and `lag = '30 seconds'` spaces the runs out.
- **Environments.** `CREATE DATABASE dev CLONE prod` makes a database that starts as prod is now, copying no data file, and its rows keep their row ids and versions. Writes to either side stay apart, and `DROP DATABASE dev` removes only what dev wrote. `WITH (schemas = (sales))` clones some schemas, and `WITH NO DATA` clones only the definitions. `ALTER DATABASE dev REFRESH orders` brings a table, and the materialized views that follow it, up to prod's present. A project is a folder of objects, migrations and tests. `pondra plan` shows what a deploy would change, and `pondra deploy` applies exactly that plan and then runs the tests. Migrations run once in each database, and a table changes in place only in ways that keep its rows. `pondra branch` and `pondra diff` give each developer a database of their own and compare it with prod, and `CALL plan(…)` and `CALL deploy(…)` do the same from any door. `pondra workspace pull` and `push` keep a lake's files in step with a folder. Secrets, shares and recipients never reach a branch or a deploy.
- **Share a table with another company.** Sharing is SQL: `CREATE SHARE acme`, `ALTER SHARE acme ADD TABLE orders`, `CREATE RECIPIENT acme_corp EXPIRES IN '90 days'`, then `GRANT SELECT ON SHARE acme TO RECIPIENT acme_corp`. The other company reads the files from the lake's storage with its own tools, such as pandas, Spark, Power BI or another Pondra, through links that last 15 minutes. It uses the open Delta Sharing protocol, so its clients work as they are. A recipient sees only what is shared, at a published version, and every request is kept in the audit log. Partitions, deletes, history and renamed columns read correctly. The console's table menu has **Share with another company…**.
- **Writes spread over every node.** `INSERT … SELECT` and `CREATE TABLE … AS` are now written by every node at once when their rows split as they are, and one commit records all their files. On three nodes sharing one 4-core machine, copying TPC-H's `lineitem` at scale factor 1 took 3.6 s, down from 5.9 s. Those whose rows don't split as they are are written from one node.
- **Sequences, identity columns, UNIQUE, enum types and indexes.** Sequences hand out each value once, even across three nodes and a leader's kill, and identity columns work the same way. `UNIQUE` is enforced by the leader on every SQL write to the table, and a duplicate fails with Postgres's code 23505. An enum column refuses labels it doesn't list (22P02), and casts to an enum and `enum_range` work. `CREATE INDEX` is kept as an object, and a notice says that nothing is built. One registry covers every kind of object: `COMMENT ON` sets a comment, `SHOW CREATE` gives the statement that makes an object again, and `pondra.objects` lists them all. `CREATE OR ALTER TABLE` brings a table to a new definition by adding columns, widening types and setting its layout, and it refuses anything that would lose or reinterpret rows.
- **DuckDB's and other databases' spellings.** Eighteen of the 22 everyday forms that failed now work, each answering as DuckDB 1.5.5 does: `PIVOT` and `UNPIVOT`, `COLUMNS('re')`, `SELECT * RENAME`, `ORDER BY ALL`, `FETCH FIRST`, list comprehensions, lambda functions, `max_by` and `arg_max`, `ASOF JOIN … ON`, `SUMMARIZE` and `USING SAMPLE`. A select's alias can be used in its `WHERE`. `TABLESAMPLE` used to be ignored and return every row, and now it samples. Spellings from DuckDB, Snowflake, Postgres and BigQuery work too, among them `VERSION AS OF` and `FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF` for time travel, `SHOW SCHEMAS`, `SHOW USERS`, `SHOW SECRETS`, and `ANALYZE` and `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW`, which dbt and BI tools send and which now succeed with nothing to do.
- **Windows as SQL, with `EMIT FINAL`.** A window is now the query's own `GROUP BY` on a time bucket, so its size is stated once: `date_bin(INTERVAL '1 minute', ts)` for minutes, or `SESSION(ts, INTERVAL '30 minutes')` for sessions. `EMIT FINAL` writes each group once, when time passes it. `lateness = '10 seconds'` says how late a row may arrive, and `idle = '1 minute'` closes a quiet stream's last group. `pondra.flows` counts late rows per view, though session views don't count theirs yet. A time bucket that only grows with time works (`date_bin`, `date_trunc`, `time_bucket`, a cast to a date), and one that repeats, such as `hour(ts)`, is refused by name. The old options form still works.
- **Vector search and model calls.** An exact top 10 of 200,000 vectors of 384 floats takes 0.063 s, against 0.154 s for DuckDB on the same 4-core machine, and returns numpy's answer. `cosine_similarity`, `cosine_distance`, `l2_distance` and `dot_product` also answer to DuckDB's and pgvector's names. `ai_complete` and `ai_embed` ask each distinct text once, send embeddings 64 to a request, and try again after a 429, a server error or a lost connection, with at most 16 model requests in flight per node. A row whose call fails for good stays NULL, and the failure is counted in the node's metrics and logged.
- **Scripts that run things at once.** `FOR … PARALLEL n`, `ASYNC`, `AWAIT ALL` and `AWAIT $h` run statements beside each other, and `AWAIT 'id'` waits for a run that `pondra.start` began. `VALUES` takes subqueries in its rows. A bare `AWAIT` waits for every run, and a bare `END` closes any block. `START CALL p(…)` starts a procedure without waiting, on every door, Postgres included. `EXECUTE IMMEDIATE FROM 'etl/x.sql'` runs a workspace file as `CALL run(…)` does, and a procedure can take defaults, as in `CREATE PROCEDURE p($n BIGINT = 5)`.
- **Task graphs.** `CREATE TASK … AFTER` and `WHEN` build task graphs, and `pondra.result` reads an earlier task's result. `WITH (retries, retry_delay, timeout, on_failure)` sets how a task retries, how long it may run and what happens when it fails. `EXECUTE TASK` runs one now, with values, and `ALTER TASK … SUSPEND` and `RESUME` pause and restart it.
- **Changed: statements that were taken quietly are refused by name.** `CREATE TABLE … LOCATION` used to drop its location and make the table inside the lake anyway. It now names `CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE … LOCATION` for files elsewhere, and `ATTACH … (TYPE delta)` or `(TYPE iceberg)` for another engine's table. `INSERT OVERWRITE` used to append and `RETURNING` used to be dropped; both are refused now, with the way to write each. A `$name` in a function that isn't one of its parameters is refused when the function is made. `INSERT OR REPLACE` now upserts only the columns it gives. The vector functions refuse two vectors of different lengths, as DuckDB and pgvector do, where they used to answer NULL.
- **Faster under load.** At 50 dashboard clients, queries answer 870 a second, up from 760. At 200 clients the 99th percentile is 0.83 s, down from 1.54 s. A writer beside 400 clients lands 19,900 rows a second, up from 2,860, and a point lookup over Postgres takes 0.16 ms, down from 0.35 ms. TPC-H and TPC-DS answers match DuckDB's, and no benchmark query got slower. Remembered answers last: a repeated query on a lake that nobody writes to is answered from memory for as long as nothing changes, and background work no longer clears it.

The details are in [`docs/prototype-status.md`](https://github.com/alimardon123/pondra/blob/main/docs/prototype-status.md) (round 33).

## Install

| You have | Run | Then |
|---|---|---|
| Windows | `irm https://github.com/alimardon123/pondra/releases/latest/download/install.ps1 \| iex` | `pondra` |
| Linux, macOS | `curl -fsSL https://github.com/alimardon123/pondra/releases/latest/download/install.sh \| sh` | `pondra` |
| Python | `pip install pondra` (add `pyarrow` for pandas, Polars and Arrow) | `pondra`, `python -m pondra`, or `import pondra` |
| Node | `npm install -g pondra` | `pondra`, or `npx pondra` with no install |
| A web page | `pondra-web.tar.gz` below: `pondra_web.js` and its `.wasm`, served from your site | `new Page()` ([Pondra in a browser](https://alimardon123.github.io/pondra/guides/browser/)) |

The files below: the binary alone for each platform (`pondra-<platform>.tar.gz` / `.zip`, what the
installers download), the Python wheels, the npm packages and the page's module (`pondra-web.tar.gz`). What changed is in the commits
below and in [`docs/prototype-status.md`](https://github.com/alimardon123/pondra/blob/main/docs/prototype-status.md).
